name: Social Proof
statement: Unsure what to do, people copy the crowd, trusting that others must know better.
statementAccent: people copy the crowd, trusting that others must know better
meaning: Social proof is a psychological and social phenomenon in which people copy the actions of others in an attempt to behave correctly in a given situation, on the assumption that the surrounding people know more about what is going on. The term was coined and popularised by Robert Cialdini in his 1984 book Influence, and it is one of his six principles of influence. It is closely tied to informational social influence and to conformity: when we are uncertain what to think or do, we treat the behaviour of others as evidence of the right response, and the more people who appear to be doing something, the more we assume it must be correct. Social proof underlies everything from following a crowd in an emergency to buying a bestseller, and it is a mainstay of marketing through testimonials, reviews, popularity labels, and endorsements.
mechanism: In ambiguous or uncertain situations people cannot easily determine the appropriate behaviour on their own, so they look to others to decide what is correct, taking the group's actions as information about reality. This is informational social influence: we conform because we believe others' reading of an unclear situation is more accurate than our own. The pull is stronger under greater uncertainty, when more people are seen doing the thing, and when those others are similar to us, since similar people seem better guides to what we should do. Classic research illuminates the mechanism: Sherif's 1935 autokinetic studies showed groups converging on shared norms when judging an ambiguous moving light; Latané and Darley's work on bystanders showed people reading others' inaction as a sign no help is needed; and Milgram, Bickman, and Berkowitz's 1969 street experiment found that the larger a crowd staring up at the sky, the more passers-by stopped to look up too, a direct demonstration that numbers amplify social proof.

examples.text: In the 1969 street experiment, the more confederates who looked up at the sky, the more passers-by stopped and looked up as well, numbers driving imitation.
Testimonials, star ratings, bestseller labels, subscriber counts, and viewing-now cues all use social proof to signal that others have chosen a product.
Recorded laughter on a comedy show cues audiences that others find it funny, nudging them to laugh and enjoy it more.

variants.name: Informational social influence
variants.text: The underlying mechanism of conforming because one believes others' interpretation of an ambiguous situation is more accurate than one's own.

variants.name: Similarity-weighted social proof
variants.text: The moderator by which the behaviour of similar others carries more weight, since people like us seem better guides to appropriate action.

whyItMatters: Social proof is one of the most powerful and pervasive forces in social behaviour, central to social psychology, marketing, and the understanding of conformity and herd behaviour. It explains how norms form, how crowds coordinate, and how uncertainty leads people to look outward for cues, for better or worse: it can spread helpful conventions and also fuel bubbles, panics, and bystander inaction. As one of Cialdini's principles of influence, it is the engine behind reviews, ratings, popularity signals, and endorsements that shape countless everyday choices, and it grows ever more potent in a networked world where visible counts of likes, followers, and purchases are ubiquitous. Recognising social proof helps explain both the wisdom and the folly of crowds, and why what others do so strongly shapes what we do.

working.text: note that when people are unsure of the right response, they look to others for cues about correct behaviour.
display evidence that many people, ideally similar ones, are doing the thing, since numbers and similarity strengthen the effect.
watch people adopt the apparent consensus behaviour, treating the crowd's action as information about what is correct.

limits: Social proof is strongest under uncertainty and weakens when people have clear information or firm personal views; it is not an irresistible force but a heuristic that can be overridden. It can also mislead, since a crowd may be wrong, ill-informed, or itself merely following others, so social proof can propagate errors, bubbles, and bystander inaction as readily as good conventions. Manufactured or fake social proof, such as bought reviews or inflated counts, can backfire when detected. Related conformity research is sometimes conflated with it, though some classic studies, like Asch's line experiments, involve normative pressure to fit in rather than informational influence. So social proof is a robust but bounded phenomenon whose direction depends entirely on what the crowd happens to be doing.
misreadings: Social proof is not simply peer pressure to fit in; at its core it is informational, people copying others because they believe others know better, which is why it operates most strongly under genuine uncertainty. It does not guarantee good outcomes, since crowds can be wrong and social proof can spread mistakes and panics. And it is not unconditional: clear personal knowledge, dissimilar sources, or detected fakery all weaken it, so treating the behaviour of others as always decisive, or as always wise, misreads a heuristic whose value depends on whether the crowd is actually a reliable guide.
origin: Coined and popularised by Robert Cialdini in his 1984 book Influence as one of the six principles of persuasion, drawing on research into informational social influence and conformity by Sherif, Latané and Darley, and Milgram and colleagues.
